meta.chapterLabel: Lesson 1: Meeting: Nice to Meet You (Extras)
meta.baseChapterLabel: Lesson 1: Meeting: Nice to Meet You

items.target: にほんじんですか
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Form job: worked example of topic omission on a question with a real noun in it. The deck's only other topicless question is the identity check たなかさんですか (Tanaka-san desu ka). Minimal pair with w2-anata-wa-nihonjin-q, hence the hints on both.
items.hint: the short form, with the topic left out
items.note: Same question as あなたはにほんじんですか (anata wa nihonjin desu ka) with the topic removed. This is the version people actually say: the pronoun sounds blunt when the person is standing in front of you.

items.target: おくにはどちらですか
items.reviewNote: Constructed by stripping the address term from the SPEAKING PRACTICE 1 question. Form job: the bare version is the one a learner will actually need, and every おくに card in the deck carries a name in front of it.
items.hint: asked straight out, with no name in front of it
items.note: The form you use once you are already in conversation. Putting a name in front, as in ホフマンさん、おくにはどちらですか (Hofuman san, okuni wa dochira desu ka), is only for catching someone's attention first.

items.target: イギリスです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: イギリス (igirisu) as a country appears in no sentence, only イギリスじん (igirisujin). Paired answer to w2-okuni-dochira-bare.
items.scene: answering the question おくにはどちらですか (okuni wa dochira desu ka) with the country on its own

items.target: はい、オーストラリアじんです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Form job: member 3 of the statement / question / reply set. Also the only Australian sentence in the deck alongside its two set-mates.
items.note: はい、そうです (hai, sou desu) would also work here. Repeating the noun is the fuller answer; そうです (sou desu) only confirms, without saying what is being confirmed.
items.scene: replying to a question that already named both the person and the nationality

items.target: たなかさんですか
items.reviewNote: GRAMMAR 4 (Omission of the topic) worked example, cited verbatim. That grammar point currently has no card of its own, and this is the shortest possible form of the lesson's central pattern. The deck jumps straight to the long すみません + company + name version.
items.note: The topic is dropped because it is obvious who is being asked. The full form would start with あなたは (anata wa), but Japanese leaves it out whenever context makes it clear, and the reply drops it too.

items.english: This is Harris-san of the Australian Embassy.
items.target: こちらはオーストラリアたいしかんのハリスさんです
items.pronunciation: kochira wa ōsutoraria taishikan no harisu san desu
items.reviewNote: Constructed from EXERCISE V's structure and EXERCISE III's Harris entry. Vocabulary job: たいしかん (taishikan) is the one work-affiliation word with no third-person introduction card, and this is the deck's only chance to show a compound where の (no) is deliberately absent.
items.note: オーストラリアたいしかん (Oosutoraria taishikan) runs together with no の (no) inside it, because the country simply says which embassy. The の (no) comes afterwards, joining the embassy to the person who works there.

items.english: I'd like to see Harris-san, please.
items.target: ハリスさんをおねがいします
items.reviewNote: Constructed on the SPEAKING PRACTICE 3 pattern. Particle job: を (o) had exactly one example in the entire lesson. Second of three.
items.note: The name takes を (o) here, not は (wa). Harris-san is what you are asking for, not what the sentence is about, and that is the whole difference between the two particles.

items.target: わたしはイギリスじんです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: わたし (watashi) appears in only one sentence card in the deck, and there it sits inside brackets, so the learner never sees it used for real.
items.note: は (wa) after わたし (watashi) makes 'I' the topic, exactly as it does after a name. Japanese drops it once it is obvious who you mean, which is why the Key Sentence prints it in brackets: （わたしは）スミスです (watashi wa Sumisu desu).

items.target: はい、にほんじんです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Form job: paired answer to w2-anata-wa-nihonjin-q, and the deck's only first-person affirmative reply. にほんじん (nihonjin) previously appeared in one statement card only.
items.note: The topic drops out of the answer for the same reason it usually drops out of the question: both of you already know who is being talked about.
items.scene: replying about yourself when someone has just asked your nationality

items.english: Nice to meet you. I am Smith of ABC Foods. I look forward to working with you.
items.target: はじめまして。ABCフーズのスミスです。よろしくおねがいします
items.pronunciation: hajimemashite. ēbīshī fūzu no sumisu desu. yoroshiku onegaishimasu
items.reviewNote: TARGET DIALOGUE, Smith's self-introduction, verbatim, and the model for EXERCISE IV. The deck has two substitutions of it (fib-c1-intro-brown, fib-c1-intro-raja) but not the original three-part introduction the book actually teaches. Contains the Roman letters ABC exactly as the book prints them; see coverageNotes.

items.target: ハリスです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: gives さん (san) its own worked minimal pair. Every self-introduction card in the deck is a long three-part greeting; this is the bare form and the first half of the pair with w2-harisu-san-desu.
items.note: Never さん (san) on your own name. さん (san) is respect you hand to other people, so attaching it to yourself sounds like you are praising yourself.
items.scene: giving your own surname when someone asks who you are, without はじめまして (hajimemashite)

items.target: いいえ、インドじんです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: first appearance of インドじん (indojin) in a sentence. Paired answer to w2-raja-japanese-q.
items.note: いいえ (iie) on its own leaves the question hanging, so the right noun follows immediately. The reply denies and corrects in one breath, which is why this lesson never needs a way to say 'is not'.
items.scene: correcting someone who has just guessed that Raja-san is Japanese

items.target: アメリカです
items.reviewNote: SPEAKING PRACTICE 1, Smith's reply, verbatim. The deck teaches the question (o-prefix-example, スミスさん、おくにはどちらですか) but not the answer, so the exchange is half taught. Prompt is close to the bare vocabulary card amerika ('United States'), hence the hint.
items.note: The topic is dropped because the question already named it. Note that the answer is the country アメリカ (Amerika), not the nationality アメリカじん (amerikajin).
items.scene: answering when asked which country you are from

items.target: ハリスさんはオーストラリアじんですか
items.pronunciation: harisu san wa ōsutorariajin desu ka
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Form job: member 2 of the statement / question / reply set, deliberately on the same vocabulary as the card before it so the transformation is visible.
items.note: The same sentence as ハリスさんはオーストラリアじんです (Harisu san wa Oosutorariajin desu) with か (ka) added. Nothing else moves: no inversion, no change of ending, no extra word.

items.target: わたしのくにはにほんです
items.pronunciation: watashi no kuni wa nihon desu
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: covers both くに (kuni) without the honorific and the country にほん (nihon), neither of which appears in any sentence. Also the clearest place to teach the お (o) / no-お contrast against the おくに questions.
items.note: No お (o) on your own くに (kuni). The honorific belongs to the other person's country, so おくに (okuni) about yourself sounds as odd as calling yourself さん (san). Note also that the answer here is the country にほん (Nihon), not the nationality にほんじん (Nihonjin).

items.english: Tanaka-san, this is Brown-san of the Bank of London.
items.target: たなかさん、こちらはロンドンぎんこうのブラウンさんです
items.pronunciation: tanaka san, kochira wa rondon ginkō no buraun san desu
items.reviewNote: Lifted verbatim from SPEAKING PRACTICE 2, Sasaki's line. Form job: the deck has the bare introduction (fib-c1-this-is-brown) but never shows how you address the listener first, which is what makes an introduction an introduction rather than a description.
items.note: Two people in one sentence doing completely different jobs. たなかさん (Tanaka-san) at the front is the person you are speaking to, marked by nothing but a comma; ブラウンさん (Buraun-san) is the person you are speaking about. Only こちら (kochira) gets は (wa).

items.target: ちゅうごくです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: ちゅうごく (chuugoku) as a country appears in no sentence. Paired answer to w2-chan-okuni-q, and a country-versus-nationality contrast against the existing Chan statement.
items.note: The country ちゅうごく (Chuugoku), not the nationality. Compare チャンさんはちゅうごくじんです (Chan san wa Chuugokujin desu): same person, but じん (jin) makes it about her rather than about the place.
items.scene: Chan-san answering the question おくにはどちらですか (okuni wa dochira desu ka)

items.english: Raja-san is with the University of Tokyo.
items.target: ラジャさんはとうきょうだいがくです
items.pronunciation: raja san wa tōkyō daigaku desu
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: だいがく (daigaku) and the affiliation-as-noun-2 pattern. The book only ever shows an affiliation in the [company] の [person] shape, so flag this if the reviewer wants to stay strictly inside what is printed.
items.note: Literally 'Raja-san is the University of Tokyo', which is how Japanese states where somebody works. です (desu) links the topic to whatever identifies it and leaves the rest to context.

items.target: ラジャさんはにほんじんですか
items.pronunciation: raja san wa nihonjin desu ka
items.reviewNote: Constructed, modelled on EXERCISE II-B. Form job: the deck has three negative-correction answers but only one question that expects a correction. This one sets up インドじん (indojin), which appears in no sentence.

items.target: チャンさんはうけつけですか
items.pronunciation: chan san wa uketsuke desu ka
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Form job: every question card in the deck asks about a nationality or an identity. This shows the question ending applying to an ordinary noun, which is the point of the rule.
items.note: The same か (ka) that turns a nationality sentence into a question does it here too, with no regard for what kind of noun sits in front of です (desu).

items.english: This is Hoffman-san of Berlin Motors.
items.target: こちらはベルリンモーターズのホフマンさんです
items.pronunciation: kochira wa berurin mōtāzu no hofuman san desu
items.reviewNote: Lifted verbatim from the EXERCISE V worked example. Form job: the deck holds a substitution built on this line (fib-c1-this-is-brown) but not the model line itself, and this is the only place ベルリンモーターズ (Berurin Mootaazu) appears in a sentence.
items.note: さん (san) stays on because you are naming somebody else. Introducing himself, the same man would say ベルリンモーターズのホフマンです (Berurin Mootaazu no Hofuman desu), with the さん (san) gone.

items.english: I am Smith of ABC Foods.
items.target: ABCフーズのスミスです
items.reviewNote: SPEAKING PRACTICE 3, Smith's first line, verbatim. The deck already has the second half of that line (onegaishimasu-pattern-ch14) but not this half, so the learner never sees the bare self-identification with an affiliation. Extends ks4-i-am-smith, which has the name only.
items.note: The [company] の (no) [name] です (desu) pattern used to state who you are, as opposed to こちらは (kochira wa) ... です, which states who someone else is.
items.scene: identifying yourself at a reception desk, without はじめまして (hajimemashite)

items.target: スミスさんはイギリスじんですか
items.pronunciation: sumisu san wa igirisujin desu ka
items.reviewNote: EXERCISE II-B model question, verbatim. The lesson's only other nationality question is ks2-smith-american-q, which expects yes; this one expects a correction, and it is the question the existing eg-no-british / fib-c1-hoffman-not-british answer cards are modelled on. Second card on this pattern, so within the cap.

items.target: インドです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: インド (indo) as a country appears in no sentence. Paired answer to w2-raja-no-okuni-q, and the last of the seven WORD POWER countries to get one.
items.note: Compare ラジャさんはインドじんです (Raja san wa Indojin desu). Dropping じん (jin) turns the answer from a description of the person into the name of a place.
items.scene: answering a question about which country Raja-san is from, with the country on its own

items.english: Nice to meet you. I am Harris of the Australian Embassy. I look forward to working with you.
items.target: はじめまして。オーストラリアたいしかんのハリスです。よろしくおねがいします
items.pronunciation: hajimemashite. ōsutoraria taishikan no harisu desu. yoroshiku onegaishimasu
items.reviewNote: EXERCISE IV item 3, verbatim. The deck built items 1 and 2 of that three-item exercise (fib-c1-intro-brown, fib-c1-intro-raja) and skipped item 3, which is also the lesson's only chance to use たいしかん (taishikan) inside a sentence rather than as a bare noun.

items.target: はい、うけつけです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Form job: closes the statement / question / reply set on うけつけ (uketsuke), mirroring the same three-step set built on オーストラリアじん (oosutorariajin) so the learner sees the pattern hold across two different kinds of noun.
items.scene: replying to a question that has already named the job

items.target: はい、そうです
items.reviewNote: TARGET DIALOGUE, Tanaka's reply, verbatim, and also the answer half of EXERCISE III's model. The deck has はい (hai) and そうです (sou desu) as separate bare vocabulary cards but never the reply itself, so all three confirm-identity question cards in the lesson currently have no answer.
items.note: NOTES 2 explains that そう (sou) stands in for the noun instead of repeating it, so you say はい、そうです (hai, sou desu) rather than はい、たなかです (hai, Tanaka desu).
items.scene: answering when someone asks if you are the person they were looking for

items.english: Excuse me, are you Raja-san of the University of Tokyo?
items.target: すみません。とうきょうだいがくのラジャさんですか
items.pronunciation: sumimasen. tōkyō daigaku no raja san desu ka
items.reviewNote: EXERCISE III item 3, reconstructed from the printed model plus the information given for that item. Vocabulary job: だいがく (daigaku) appears in one sentence in the whole deck, and never in a question.

items.target: あなたはにほんじんですか
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: あなた (anata) appears in no sentence in the deck, only as a bare word and as a speaker label in the exercises. Half of a minimal pair with w2-nihonjin-q-bare.
items.hint: with あなた (anata) spelled out as the topic
items.note: Grammatically complete, and the version worth learning first because you can see every part. In real conversation the pronoun is usually dropped or replaced by the person's name.

items.target: うけつけをおねがいします
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Particle job: third example of を (o), and the only one where the thing marked is not a person, so the particle is not learned as part of a fixed person-shaped phrase. The book's note only shows 'person を おねがいします', so this widens it slightly.
items.note: を (o) marks whatever you are asking for, and that does not have to be a person. Said at an entrance or on the phone when you do not know who you need yet.
items.scene: asking to be put through to the front desk rather than to a named person

items.target: ハリスさんのおくにはどちらですか
items.pronunciation: harisu san no okuni wa dochira desu ka
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Particle job: の (no) had ten examples in the deck and all ten were [company] の [person]. This is the first with an ordinary noun after it, and the question half of the pair that puts オーストラリア (Oosutoraria) in a sentence.
items.note: Asking a third party about someone rather than asking the person directly, so の (no) links the name to おくに (okuni). Every other の (no) in this lesson joins a company to a person; here it is plain possession.

items.english: Hoffman-san, what country are you from?
items.target: ホフマンさん、おくにはどちらですか
items.pronunciation: hofuman san, okuni wa dochira desu ka
items.reviewNote: Constructed on the SPEAKING PRACTICE 1 model. Particle job: どちら (dochira) and the おくに question had exactly one example in the deck. Question half of the pair that finally puts ドイツ (Doitsu) in a sentence.
items.note: The name at the front is just how you get someone's attention, so it takes a comma and no particle. The topic marker は (wa) goes on おくに (okuni), which is what the sentence is actually about. どちら (dochira) stays where the answer will go instead of jumping to the front the way 'what' does in English.

items.target: ドイツです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: ドイツ (doitsu) as a country appears in no sentence in the deck, only ドイツじん (doitsujin). Paired answer to w2-hoffman-okuni-q.
items.note: Just the country plus です (desu). おくには (okuni wa) is not repeated because the question already supplied it, and the country ドイツ (Doitsu) is used rather than ドイツじん (Doitsujin) because the question asked about a place.
items.scene: Hoffman-san answering the question おくにはどちらですか (okuni wa dochira desu ka)

items.target: ホフマンさんはイギリスじんですか
items.pronunciation: hofuman san wa igirisujin desu ka
items.reviewNote: EXERCISE II-B item 1, reconstructed by putting ホフマンさん (Hofuman-san) into the printed model スミスさんはイギリスじんですか. Form job: the deck already holds this drill's answer card (fib-c1-hoffman-not-british, 'No, he is German.') with no question attached to it. Place this immediately BEFORE that card rather than at the anchor id below.

items.target: チャンさんはちゅうごくじんです
items.reviewNote: EXERCISE I item 3, verbatim. Flagged low because the statement pattern already has two cards (ks1-smith-american, wa-particle-example); the only argument for it is that ちゅうごくじん (chuugokujin) otherwise never appears in a sentence anywhere in the lesson. Prune freely.

items.english: Brown-san is with the Bank of London.
items.target: ブラウンさんはロンドンぎんこうです
items.pronunciation: buraun san wa rondon ginkō desu
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: ぎんこう (ginkou) outside the [company] の [person] frame. Same caveat as the University of Tokyo card, and the two are best kept or cut together.
items.note: The other way to link a person to a company. ロンドンぎんこうのブラウンさん (Rondon ginkou no Buraun-san) makes the person the point of the phrase; this makes the company the news.

items.target: ラジャさんのおくにはどちらですか
items.pronunciation: raja san no okuni wa dochira desu ka
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Particle job: second example of の (no) joining a person to an ordinary noun, and the question half of the pair that puts インド (Indo) in a sentence.

items.target: チャンさんはうけつけです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: うけつけ (uketsuke) appears in no sentence in the deck; the book only ever uses it as a speaker label. Chan is the one cast member the book gives no workplace to, so no printed fact is contradicted, but swap the name if the reviewer would rather keep her unemployed.
items.note: Noun 2 after は (wa) does not have to be a nationality. Anything that identifies the topic works, and a job identifies a person just as well as a country does.

items.target: ハリスさんです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: the second half of a minimal pair with w2-harisu-desu, differing only in さん (san). The deck teaches the さん rule in a note on the bare vocabulary card but never shows the two sentences side by side.
items.note: The same name with さん (san) added is now about somebody else. Compare ハリスです (Harisu desu), which can only mean 'I am Harris'. This one syllable is the whole difference between talking about yourself and talking about another person.
items.scene: telling someone which of the people in front of you is the one they were looking for

items.english: Nice to meet you. I am Tanaka.
items.target: はじめまして。たなかです
items.reviewNote: TARGET DIALOGUE, Tanaka's reply, verbatim. Every self-introduction card in the deck names a company; this is the only place the book shows the short form, and it is also the one a learner outside a business setting would actually use.
items.note: Note there is no さん (san) on your own name. Tanaka drops the company here because Smith had already named it when asking for him.
items.scene: introducing yourself with just your name

items.target: オーストラリアです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: オーストラリア (oosutoraria) as a standalone country appears in no sentence, only inside the compound オーストラリアたいしかん (Oosutoraria taishikan). Paired answer to w2-harris-no-okuni-q.
items.note: The country, not the nationality. Compare ハリスさんはオーストラリアじんです (Harisu san wa Oosutorariajin desu), which describes the man rather than the place.
items.scene: answering a question about which country Harris-san is from, with the country on its own

items.target: いいえ、ちがいます
items.reviewNote: NOTES 2 teaches this phrase in so many words ('When replying in the negative, say いいえ、ちがいます'), yet ちがいます (chigaimasu) appears nowhere in the deck. The English gloss is mine, as the book prints the phrase untranslated inside the note.
items.note: The negative counterpart of はい、そうです (hai, sou desu). Use it to deny the identification outright. When you want to correct it instead, give the right noun: いいえ、アメリカじんです (iie, amerikajin desu).
items.scene: answering no when asked whether you are a particular person

items.target: ラジャさんはインドじんです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: gives インドじん (indojin) a statement as well as a reply, so the learner can produce it without a question to lean on.
items.note: The plain statement underneath the correction: once the mistake in いいえ、インドじんです (iie, Indojin desu) has been fixed, this is what you would say from scratch.

items.english: Excuse me, are you Tanaka-san of the Nozomi Department Store?
items.target: すみません。のぞみデパートのたなかさんですか
items.pronunciation: sumimasen. nozomi depāto no tanaka san desu ka
items.reviewNote: TARGET DIALOGUE, Smith's opening line, verbatim. The deck has two substitution drills built on this sentence (fib-c1-confirm-hoffman, fib-c1-confirm-brown) but not the model line they were derived from. That makes three cards on one pattern, which I would normally avoid, but the book's own dialogue line is the one worth keeping if the owner prunes.

items.target: ハリスさんはオーストラリアじんです
items.reviewNote: Constructed. Vocabulary job: オーストラリアじん (oosutorariajin) appears in no sentence anywhere in the deck. Also member 1 of a form contrast set (statement / question / reply) built on one piece of vocabulary.
items.note: オーストラリアじん (Oosutorariajin) is the country オーストラリア (Oosutoraria) with じん (jin), 'person of', stuck on the end. Every nationality in this lesson is built the same way.

items.english: Chan-san, what country are you from?
items.target: チャンさん、おくにはどちらですか
items.pronunciation: chan san, okuni wa dochira desu ka
items.reviewNote: Constructed on the SPEAKING PRACTICE 1 model. Particle job: second practice of the address-plus-おくに structure, and the question half of the pair that puts ちゅうごく (chuugoku) in a sentence.

items.english: I look forward to working with you as well.
items.target: こちらこそ、よろしくおねがいします
items.reviewNote: TARGET DIALOGUE, Tanaka's closing line, verbatim. The deck has こちらこそ (kochirakoso) as a bare vocabulary card and よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu) as another, but never the combined reply, which is the only form the book actually uses it in.
items.note: こちらこそ (kochirakoso) is what turns the phrase into a reply, carrying the 'as well'. Compare the plain よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu), which is what you say first.
items.scene: replying after the other person has said it to you first

items.target: いいえ、アメリカじんです
items.reviewNote: EXERCISE II-B model answer, verbatim, and the reply to ex2b-smith-british-q above. Prompt is close to eg-yes-american ('Yes, (he is) American.'), so the hint disambiguates. This is the third negative-correction answer in the lesson (after eg-no-british and fib-c1-hoffman-not-british); it earns its place only as the paired answer, so prune it together with its question if at all.
items.scene: correcting someone who guessed Smith-san was British
